Every outbound network call must have an explicit, deliberately-chosen timeout/cancellation policy, and that policy must be applied consistently across all code paths, including fallbacks. A common bug pattern is a primary request that is correctly bounded while a fallback or secondary call uses a bare `fetch`/socket with no timeout at all, so a host that drops packets (instead of refusing) hangs the fallback forever and blocks the caller (e.g. task start). Audit every network call on a path, not just the first one, and attach an `AbortSignal` with a sane deadline to each.

Do not reuse one-size-fits-all idle/read timeouts when the operation's expected duration genuinely varies. If a request (e.g. streaming from a local model server) can legitimately take longer than the default idle timeout, use a dedicated no-timeout/long-timeout path for that case only, and keep the default bounded timeout for everything else. When special-casing "local" endpoints, get the address matching right: include all loopback/unspecified forms (`127.0.0.0/8`, `0.0.0.0`, `::1`, IPv4-mapped IPv6 like `::ffff:127.0.0.1`), and make sure any proxy bypass rule you need (e.g. never proxy loopback) is preserved independently of the timeout change — don't let a timeout override implicitly route previously-direct loopback traffic through a proxy agent.

When a client-side timeout fires, treat it as "unknown outcome," not "operation failed." The request may have already been committed by the server, so blindly retrying (especially writes) can duplicate side effects. Prefer designs where the client either waits for the server's definitive answer with no artificial deadline when correctness depends on it (bounding only the UI-visible wait, not the underlying request), or probes current state / treats the command as read-then-decide before retrying, rather than re-executing the original call on timeout. Also reconsider whether a dropped connection should cancel in-flight requests immediately or allow a brief reconnect grace period before giving up, and make that choice explicit and tested rather than incidental.

Example: a provider fetch helper should pass an `AbortSignal` with a fixed deadline on its primary call and on any fallback call it makes; a local-server detector should match `0.0.0.0`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, and `::ffff:127.0.0.1` the same way; and a command-timeout handler should verify liveness via a bounded health probe before tearing down a connection, rather than assuming the command failed and retrying it outright.
